Three strings joined end to end along a dotted line, thin, medium and thick, labelled Z₁, Z₂ and Z₃, the middle one's length marked L, a wave arriving along the first string from the left, and a dashed arrow pointing back to the left that ends in a question mark

Welcome toJoining Two Strings

Three strings, one tension, a wave from the left — how much comes back?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: waves on three strings joined end to end

Source

Concept
Three ideal strings under one tension τ are joined end to end along a line: a first string of impedance Z₁ (x < 0), a middle string of impedance Z₂ and length L (0 < x < L), and a last string of impedance Z₃ = 9Z₁. Each impedance is Z = √(τμ) = τ/v, with μ the mass per unit length and v the wave speed. A harmonic wave of angular frequency ω arrives along the first string from the left, and the strings are drawn in the steady state, with every reflection back and forth within the middle string already present. The row beneath the first string shows the whole reflected wave (solid) and, with the middle string in place, its first two parts (dashed): the wave reflected at x = 0 and the wave back from x = L after one round trip.
Measured
ℛP = |ℛ|² is the fraction of the incident power that is reflected, ℛ being the amplitude reflection coefficient of the whole arrangement. It is plotted against ω/ωq over the frequency steps you have visited with the middle string in place; the dashed line is its level with the strings joined directly. ωq is the frequency at which the middle string is a quarter of a wavelength long.
Controls
Frequency ω/ωq from 0.10 to 4.00. Z₂/Z₁ from 1.5 to 6.0, greyed while the middle string is removed; changing Z₂ recuts the middle string to L = 3ℓZ₁/Z₂ (ℓ is its length at Z₂ = 3Z₁), so ωq and the outer strings stay as they were. The middle-string selector puts it in place or removes it, the last string then running back to x = 0. ↻ Reset restores ω/ωq = 1.00, Z₂/Z₁ = 3.0, the middle string removed, and clears the traced curve.
Model & scale
Small slopes, no damping, one tension for all three strings. Positions and displacements share one scale, the incident amplitude 𝒜 being drawn as 0.375ℓ. At 1× speed, screen time is slowed: one period lasts 3 s at ωq and 3ωq/ω seconds in general.
Serves
Explaining, in terms of the waves reflected at the two ends of the middle string, how the power reflected depends on the frequency and on the impedance of the middle string.
Inquiry
Five questions: putting the middle string in place, comparing the two dashed waves, sweeping the frequency from 1.00 to 4.00, and changing Z₂/Z₁ at ωq; then a closing card stating the matching condition.
Misconception
Carried by the answer choices of the five questions; not stated here, so that it cannot prompt an answer.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Commit before revealCard 1 is answered before the middle string goes in; cards 3–5 ask you to make the change and read ℛP; the curve exists only over frequencies you have visited.
Evaluate afterEvery answer returns an explanation in terms of the two junctions, written for the choice picked.
Misconception targeted structurallyEach wrong option encodes a belief a student really holds; it is answered only when chosen, never shown as standing text.
What stays fixedThe dashed directly-joined level, the fixed axes, ωq and the outer strings stay put while the frequency and Z₂ change.
Operational quantitiesℛP is read to four decimals so that small non-zero values never read as zero; ω/ωq and Z₂/Z₁ are exact slider steps.
No lookup leakNo special frequency, zero or band is marked on the plot, and no number or phase annotation sits beside the waves.
One honest scaleStrings and reflected waves share one vertical scale; the recut middle string visibly changes length at that scale.
Formal layer on demandThe equations live in The Physics sheet, not on the picture.
Joining Two Strings through a Third
Three strings under one tension
Fraction of the incident power reflected

Guided Inquiry

1 · A second junction

With the middle string removed and ω/ωq at 1.00, ℛP reads 0.6400. What does ℛP read when the middle string, of impedance Z₂ = 3Z₁, is put in place?

2 · The two dashed waves

At ω/ωq = 1.00, beneath the first string, how does the grey dashed wave (reflected at x = 0) compare with the blue dashed wave (back from x = L after one round trip)?

3 · Sweeping to 2.00

Keeping Z₂/Z₁ at 3.0, move the frequency slowly from 1.00 to 2.00, watching ℛP and the curve being traced. What does ℛP read at ω/ωq = 2.00?

4 · Sweeping on to 4.00

Continue slowly from ω/ωq = 2.00 to 4.00. What does ℛP do over this range?

5 · A heavier middle string

At ω/ωq = 1.00, move Z₂/Z₁ from 3.0 to 5.0, halfway between the impedances of the first and last strings, and notice the middle string shorten as it gets heavier. What does ℛP read?

6 · Quarter-wave matching

A middle string a quarter of a wavelength long sends the wave back from its far end in antiphase with the wave reflected at its near end. With every later round trip included, they cancel only when the two junctions reflect equally, Z₂/Z₁ = Z₃/Z₂, that is Z₂ = √(Z₁Z₃) = 3Z₁. Then the first string meets Z₂²/Z₃ = Z₁ and nothing is reflected. The match holds only near ωq and its odd multiples; at even multiples the middle string has no effect at all.

Joining Two Strings through a Third

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A harmonic wave runs along a first string towards a last string whose impedance is Z₃ = 9Z₁. You can put a middle string of impedance Z₂ between them or take it out, and the sim plots the fraction ℛP of the incident power that is reflected against the frequency.

What you'll learn

  • How the first string responds to whatever lies beyond x = 0.
  • How the waves reflected at the two ends of the middle string combine.
  • How the reflected fraction depends on the frequency and on Z₂.
The set-up: three strings under one tension, joined end to end.

What's on screen

  • Three strings under one tension: the incident wave arriving on the first string, with the other strings to the right.
  • Row beneath the first string: the whole reflected wave, and with the middle string in place its first two parts, dashed.
  • Lower plot: ℛP against ω/ωq for the steps you have visited, and a dashed line for the strings joined directly.
  • Readout: the reflected fraction ℛP.
See itLook at the strings as the sim opens. Watch for: the incident wave on the first string, and the readout ℛP in the Readouts.

03

The first string reflects as if it ended on a load Zin

Joined directly, strings of impedance Z₁ and Z₃ reflect the fraction [(Z₁ − Z₃)/(Z₁ + Z₃)]² of the incident power, which is 0.64 for Z₃ = 9Z₁. The sim draws this as the dashed line.

With a middle string in 0 < x < L, the first string meets only the ratio of the force F = −τ ∂y/∂x to the velocity at x = 0. Call it Zin. The first string then reflects as if it ended on a device of impedance Zin, so that ℛ = (Z₁ − Zin)/(Z₁ + Zin) and ℛP = |ℛ|². In the middle string a wave reflects at x = L with ℛ₂₃ = (Z₂ − Z₃)/(Z₂ + Z₃) and gives Zin in terms of k₂, the wavenumber there:

Notes (4.34) and (4.35). The notes write the reflection coefficient of the whole arrangement as ℛ.
See itTake the middle string out. Watch for: the readout ℛP = 0.6400, at any frequency you leave set.
04

At a quarter wavelength the section presents Z₂²/Z₃

Let the middle string be a quarter of a wavelength long, k₂L = π/2, so that e−2ik₂L = −1. Then (4.35) collapses, and Zin equals Z₁ when Z₂ is the geometric mean of Z₁ and Z₃ (4.36, 4.37):

Notes (4.36) and (4.37). All three strings share the tension, so this is also μ₂ = √(μ₁μ₃).

With Z₃ = 9Z₁ the middle string needs Z₂ = 3Z₁, the sim’s opening value. The first string then meets its own impedance, nothing is reflected, and ℛP reads 0.0000 at ω/ωq = 1.00. All the incident power passes into the last string.

See itPut the middle string in place at Z₂ = 3Z₁ and ω/ωq = 1.00. Watch for: the readout falling from 0.6400 to 0.0000.
05

The first two reflections arrive in antiphase

The wave back from x = L after one round trip is the second part of the reflected wave. The wave reflected at x = 0 is the first part. They are the grey and blue dashed waves in the sim. For Z₂ = 3Z₁ each junction reflects with −0.5, since Z₃/Z₂ = Z₂/Z₁ = 3.

The first two reflected waves at ωq, as amplitudes in units of the incident amplitude.

The wave from x = L has crossed x = 0 twice, so its amplitude is smaller, 0.375. The round trip is half a wavelength at ωq, which reverses it. The two leave −0.125.

The waves that bounce back and forth inside the middle string, each weaker than the last, supply the missing +0.125 and the total is exactly zero. At 2ωq the round trip is a whole wavelength, the first two are in step, and the total returns to −0.8, so ℛP = 0.64.

See itPut the middle string in place at Z₂ = 3Z₁ and ω/ωq = 1.00. Watch for: the grey and blue dashed waves under the first string in antiphase, the blue one smaller.
06

The match returns at odd multiples of ωq

At other frequencies Zin follows the general (4.35). With Z₂ = 3Z₁ the curve is zero at ωq and again at 3ωq, where the section is an odd number of quarter wavelengths long.

ℛP for Z₂ = 3Z₁. The sim draws this curve as you step through the frequencies.

At 2ωq and 4ωq the section is a whole number of half wavelengths long and has no effect, so ℛP is back at 0.6400, on the dashed line.

The quiet band is narrow. Near ωq, ℛP stays under 0.1 only from 0.84 to 1.16.

See itPut the middle string in place at Z₂ = 3Z₁ and ω/ωq = 2.00. Watch for: ℛP back at 0.6400.
07

Only Z₂ = √(Z₁Z₃) matches

A quarter-wave section presents Z₂²/Z₃, not Z₂. At ωq that equals Z₁ only for Z₂ = 3Z₁.

ℛP at ωq for each Z₂ the slider allows.

Halfway between Z₁ and Z₃ is Z₂ = 5Z₁. The section is still a quarter wavelength long at ωq, but it presents 25Z₁/9 = 2.78Z₁, so ℛ = −0.471 and ℛP = (16/34)² = 0.2215. That is less than 0.64, and not zero.

Across the slider’s range, 1.5Z₁ to 6Z₁, ℛP at ωq stays below 0.64, and only the geometric mean brings it to zero.

See itMove Z₂/Z₁ to 5.0 at ω/ωq = 1.00. Watch for: the middle string shorter, and ℛP reading 0.2215.
08

Where it matters

  • Ultrasound. Layers a quarter of a wavelength thick are put on the faces of transducers that send ultrasound into the body, to clear the reflection at the design frequency.
  • Optical coatings. A coating a quarter of a wavelength thick, with refractive index n₂ = √(n₁n₃), removes the reflection of one colour at normal incidence. It has the same form as Z₂ = √(Z₁Z₃).
  • A narrow band. One section matches only near its design frequency and its odd multiples. A wide band needs several sections.
09

Summary

In one line. Three strings are joined end to end, and this sim lets you put a middle string in or take it out and read the fraction of the incident power that is reflected, against frequency.

Key points

  • The first string reflects as if it ended on a load Zin, with ℛ = (Z₁ − Zin)/(Z₁ + Zin).
  • A quarter-wave section presents Z₂²/Z₃, which is Z₁ for Z₂ = √(Z₁Z₃).
  • The match holds at ωq and its odd multiples. At even multiples the section has no effect.

Common mix-ups

  • “Two junctions must reflect more than one.” At ωq with Z₂ = 3Z₁ the readout falls from 0.6400 to 0.0000, since the two reflected waves cancel.
  • “Any quarter-wave section matches.” At Z₂ = 5Z₁ the section is still a quarter wavelength, and ℛP reads 0.2215.
  • “Once matched, the frequency no longer matters.” At 2ωq the readout is back at 0.6400.

Things to try on your own

  • With Z₂ = 3Z₁ in place, read ℛP at ω/ωq = 1, 2, 3 and 4.
  • At ω/ωq = 1.00, step Z₂/Z₁ from 1.5 to 6.0 and note where ℛP is smallest.
  • Take the middle string out and sweep the frequency, then compare with the dashed line.
